---
title: "Ranking noisy estimates"
subtitle: "1.3 · a simulated league, after Walters' teaching slides"
description: "Effects of unequal sampling precision on the extreme positions of a ranking."
---

Thirty simulated units are ranked by their estimates, with the largest first. Each estimate is a fixed true value
plus sampling error; units with fewer observations have larger standard errors (SEs). Less precise units tend to be
overrepresented at both extremes. The initial dataset and twenty repetitions illustrate this effect and its
variation between datasets. The true values remain fixed.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **First draw.** Of the 10 extreme positions by estimate, small units hold 5, medium units 4 and large units 1 in this
  draw; by true value they hold 3 small, 4 medium and 3 large units.
- **True values.** In the first draw, of the top 10 by estimate, 9 are in the true top 10 (7.45 on average over the
  twenty replays). U19, a small unit with true rank 11, is the first of the bottom five: this displacement is due to sampling error.
  U18, a large unit with true rank 30, sits two rows above them: noisier small and medium units fell past it, and its
  own estimate came out above its true value.
- **Twenty replays.** The draw menu brings any replay into the table. On average over the 20 replays, small units hold
  4.35 of the 10 extreme positions and large units 2.00, and the estimates order 83.90 of the 435 pairs the wrong way,
  against 88.12 expected over many draws.
- **Replay 11.** The effect varies between repetitions: here small units hold 2, medium units 5 and large units 3, as many large
  units as by true value. The stated effect concerns average positions across repetitions.
- **Extremes highlighted.** When true values are hidden, the shaded rows do not identify which units have genuinely extreme values. In the replay chart, against the truth, 3 small and 3 large units (dashed line), small units sit
  above it in most replays and large units on it or below.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Real units have unknown true values, so this check is not possible. The firms of Kline, Rose and Walters
(2024), KRW, came with SEs of very different sizes: the race estimates have SEs from .025 to .444 (Section V.B; talk
slides 47–49). Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700, and deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1;
CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only; as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw),
changes noted; no endorsement by the authors is implied. The data describe KRW's correspondence experiment, not any
firm's current conduct. postrank's input is a posterior, not a list of estimates.
:::
